profiles.meeting_scenario: A brainstorming meeting between two faculty collaborators designing the next offering of an undergraduate software engineering course built around a shared social-media codebase maintained across semesters. Context: last year's pilot had multiple student teams contribute to one evolving application, and the department now wants a stronger, publishable version of the course model that better demonstrates students' experience with multi-team coordination and legacy-code modification. Agenda: generate and screen ideas for how the next course run should structure team boundaries, handoff practices, repository workflows, and what evidence to collect for a follow-up paper. Expected outcome: a shortlist of course-design ideas to prototype before the semester starts, along with a rough shared sense of how the course will preserve continuity across teams and across semesters.

members.name: Dr. Lena Park
members.expertise: software engineering education, agile pedagogy, curriculum design
members.background: Lena has run the department's software engineering course for four years and led the first pilot where several student teams worked on one shared application; she is comfortable with classroom logistics and assessment design, and she wants the next iteration to be credible as both a teaching intervention and a publishable educational study.
members.private_state: She wants a design that is administratively manageable for 70 students, produces clean evidence for a teaching paper, and avoids repeating the chaos of last semester's late-stage merge conflicts; she is especially concerned about preserving enough continuity that next year's students truly inherit a usable codebase.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the course should simulate 'multi-team development,' the important thing is that all teams contribute into one continuously shared trunk during the semester rather than maintaining isolated code for long periods.

A 'legacy codebase' means software produced by a previous semester's students, because the pedagogical value comes from inheriting peer-written code with imperfect documentation across course cohorts.

If teams provide 'integration demos,' those demos should prove that code is merged into the central application and runnable in the main deployment path, not just shown inside a team's own branch or environment.

A 'lightweight contribution policy' still includes required architectural notes and service-interface updates in the repository, because future cohorts need artifacts that survive instructor turnover.

members.name: Marco Alvarez
members.role: Senior teaching engineer and DevOps mentor
members.expertise: CI/CD, repository workflows, developer onboarding, industry team practices
members.background: Marco joined the department from industry two years ago, supports the course infrastructure, and mentors student teams on Git, testing, and release practices; he tends to think in terms of realistic engineering workflows and reducing friction so students can build momentum quickly.
members.private_state: He wants students to experience something closer to modern product squads, minimize operational bottlenecks on the teaching staff, and avoid brittle cross-team dependencies that stall progress; he is also trying to keep infrastructure support work within what one teaching engineer can actually maintain.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the course should simulate 'multi-team development,' the realistic version is several semi-autonomous squads owning stable slices of the product and integrating at planned checkpoints rather than constantly sharing one live trunk.
A 'legacy codebase' can include code written earlier in the same semester by another team, because onboarding into unfamiliar code matters more than whether the authors were from a prior cohort.
If teams provide 'integration demos,' that is sufficient if they show their feature working against agreed contracts in a staging setup, even if the code has not yet landed in the main branch.

A 'lightweight contribution policy' means keeping documentation overhead minimal and relying on repository conventions, pull request templates, and CI checks rather than requiring separate architectural writeups for every change.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the course should give students real experience with 'multi-team development.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means multiple teams committing into one common code line throughout the semester, so students repeatedly experience concurrent changes, merge pressure, and shared ownership.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means multiple product squads working in parallel on separate bounded areas with scheduled integration, so students experience coordination without constant repository collision.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds standard and mutually endorsed in software engineering education, and both views are plausible variants of industry practice, so each hears confirmation rather than a need to disambiguate.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss giving students practice working on 'the legacy codebase.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is specifically referring to the repository inherited from the previous year's class, including their schema decisions, naming conventions, and incomplete documentation.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is mostly picturing code that another current-semester team built in an earlier sprint, which is 'legacy enough' for onboarding and maintenance exercises.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In software teams, 'legacy' is often used loosely for any unfamiliar inherited code, so the same noun can point to different artifacts without sounding inconsistent.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both want each iteration to end with an 'integration demo.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes an integration demo only counts if the feature is merged into the main course application and runs through the shared deployment path that future teams will inherit.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes an integration demo counts if a team demonstrates the feature working with mock or staging dependencies and passing contract checks, even before main-branch merge.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both standards sound professionally legitimate and use the same evaluative language of 'integration'; in a brainstorming meeting, people usually treat the term as settled shorthand rather than unpacking the acceptance threshold.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they want a 'lightweight contribution policy' so students are not buried in process.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the policy still covers mandatory architecture decision notes, API/interface documentation updates, and handoff comments needed for the next semester's cohort.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the policy is limited to branch naming, pull request templates, tests, and CI gates, with most explanatory material kept optional to reduce student overhead.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They agree on the same high-level goal of reducing process burden, but each silently draws the boundary of 'lightweight' around a different set of required artifacts.

turns.inner_thought: If we run this again, I need the design to be tighter than last year's pilot. The publishable angle depends on showing a coherent multi-team development model, not just a collection of student projects that occasionally touched each other. For me that means one shared code line that teams are continuously contributing to, so we can study coordination, merge pressure, and shared ownership in a credible way. I also need the logistics to stay manageable for 70 students and to avoid another end-of-semester integration disaster.
turns.utterance: I think for the next run we should make the course's multi-team development model much more intentional. If we're going to write a follow-up paper, we need a structure that's not only workable in class but also clearly defensible as a teaching design.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, exactly—if we want this to feel real, students should work like semi-autonomous squads with clearer ownership, not all stepping on each other from week one. The realistic version of multi-team development is parallel teams with bounded areas and planned coordination points. That'll also keep support load from exploding on my side and reduce the number of emergency repo interventions.
turns.utterance: I agree. One thing that would help is giving student squads clearer slices of the app to own, so the multi-team development experience feels realistic without overwhelming them right at the start.

turns.inner_thought: We should ground them immediately in the actual repository inherited from last year's class. That's the legacy codebase I care about: prior-cohort code with odd naming, half-finished comments, and real continuity challenges. If they read that before scoping new work, they'll understand they're entering an existing system rather than starting fresh.
turns.utterance: Yes, and I would start the semester by having them read through the legacy codebase before they define team plans. That gives them a common baseline and makes the handoff aspect visible from the beginning.

turns.inner_thought: That pairs nicely with letting teams inherit code from each other during the semester. To me, that's also the legacy codebase once another squad has moved on from it. If they switch into partially finished modules after Sprint 1, they get repeat practice onboarding into unfamiliar code without us depending entirely on whatever last year's class left behind.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. We could even reinforce it by having each team inherit a partially finished module from another team after Sprint 1, so they repeatedly practice stepping into the legacy codebase instead of only doing it once.

turns.inner_thought: I need a routine that forces visible convergence into the shared application every cycle. An integration demo should mean the work is actually in the central app and runnable through the real path the next cohort will inherit, not just shown in isolation. That's essential both pedagogically and for clean evidence in the paper.
turns.utterance: I also think every iteration should end with an integration demo, so teams are showing not just feature progress but how their work fits into the evolving shared application.

turns.inner_thought: Absolutely. If we define integration demos around staging and contract verification, we can keep the schedule sane and avoid blocking every team on a single branch at the end of each sprint. They can prove compatibility before final merge, which is much more maintainable for me and still feels like a solid engineering practice.
turns.utterance: Definitely. To make those integration demos easier to schedule across several squads, we could lean on staging environments and contract checks so teams can show their work in a consistent way.

turns.inner_thought: We need process guardrails, but not a bureaucracy students will resent. Still, lightweight can't mean disposable. I need required architectural notes, interface updates, and handoff context committed in the repo so next year's students can actually use what gets built, even if instructors change.
turns.utterance: On the process side, I do think the class needs a lightweight contribution policy so repository work stays manageable while still preserving continuity for future cohorts.

turns.inner_thought: Good—lightweight should mean we keep it to the essentials students will actually follow: PR templates, branch naming, test expectations, CI gates. If we ask for too much extra writing, they'll stop treating the workflow as real and start treating it as compliance theater. I need something one teaching engineer can support without chasing documentation debt every week.
turns.utterance: Yes, and I think that can be pretty straightforward: a lightweight contribution policy built around pull request templates, branch conventions, and CI checks would give them enough structure with minimal friction.

turns.inner_thought: A rotating maintainer could help keep everyone feeding into the common code line and make coordination pressure explicit instead of accidental. It would also create accountability for preserving the inherited repository across cohorts. If someone in each cycle watches coherence centrally, we may avoid the late-stage merge chaos from last time.
turns.utterance: Another idea is a rotating cross-team maintainer role. That person could help keep the shared codebase coherent and give students a more genuine sense of multi-team development pressure as they work through the term.

turns.inner_thought: That role could work well if it's mainly about coordination at planned checkpoints rather than someone constantly policing everybody's day-to-day commits. They could prepare demo-ready branches, line up handoffs, and make the integration demos run smoothly without turning into a bottleneck on mainline work.
turns.utterance: I like that. We could have the maintainers focus mostly on coordinating handoffs at planned checkpoints and getting demo-ready branches in shape for the integration demos.

turns.inner_thought: Whatever else we do, I need durable artifacts for the next cohort. When students inherit the legacy codebase next year, they should find design notes, interface updates, and enough rationale to understand why things look the way they do. Otherwise continuity is fake and the teaching claim falls apart.
turns.utterance: And whatever structure we choose, I want students leaving behind documentation that future students can actually use when they next pick up the legacy codebase.

turns.inner_thought: This is a good shortlist: squad ownership, inherited code, integration demos, and a contribution policy that doesn't bog them down. I think we can pilot all of that in the syllabus draft and then work out the tooling details later. As long as the process stays lean enough to run with our staffing, this feels viable.
turns.utterance: So, as a first shortlist, it sounds like we're converging on squad ownership, inherited code work, end-of-iteration integration demos, and a lightweight contribution policy. We can turn those into a pilot structure for the syllabus draft and see where the operational details need tightening.
